title: 47 Student consumption preferences of various meat and meat-type products: A university wide survey
content:
Abstract
Meat and meat-type products critically influence our omnivore diet by providing a high-quality source of protein and essential minerals and vitamins. Over the past decade, consumer behavior towards meat and meat-type products has become less predictable and subsequent consumer demand prioritizes lifestyle choices based upon animal welfare, product health, and environmental impact. For the meat science industry to remain profitable and meet the ever-demanding concerns of the consumer, it is crucial for us to understand the dynamics that drive consumer perceptions of meat products. Therefore, the objective of this study was to determine the consumption preferences of various meat and meat-type products by Sam Houston State University (SHSU) students. Students (n = 478) enrolled at SHSU, during the Fall 2024 semester, completed an online survey instrument through the platform Qualtrics. The survey instrument consisted of demographic and 5-point Likert-scale questions relative to consumption preferences. Subsequent respondent data was analyzed using JMP with fixed effects of student classification (Freshman(FR), Sophomore(SO), Junior(JR), Senior(SR), Graduate Student(GS)). Student respondent gender consisted of 73.1% female, 24.9% male and 1.8% non-binary. Respondents consisted of 27% FR and SR, 17% SO, 26% JR and 3% GS. Students dietary eating preferences were as follows: 94.2% Omnivore, 2.4% Carnivore, 1.3% Pescatarian and 0.5% Vegetarian. Student classification did not impact (P ≥ 0.32) the weekly consumption frequency of beef, pork, lamb, goat, seafood, or poultry derived meat products. Students averaged the highest frequency of consumption (P ≤ 0.01) for poultry type products, reporting consumption around 4 – 7 times/week. Freshman students reported a greater preference (P ≤ 0.01) for consuming lab generated meat as compared to all other student classifications. Approximately half of student respondents somewhat agreed or strongly agreed to a preference for consuming traditionally or conventionally raised meat products (31.2% and 21.9%, respectively). Approximately 50% of students reported they neither agreed nor disagreed with a preference to consume specially labeled meat products such as “USDA Organic”, “Antibiotic Free”, or “Natural”. Freshman and SO students agreed to a greater degree that (P ≤ 0.01) “USDA Organic” or “Antibiotic Free” labeled meat products provide a healthier diet than conventionally raised meat products. Graduate students perceived the greatest familiarity (P ≤ 0.04) towards conventionally raised meat products, with SR, JR and SO being intermediate and FR exhibiting the least familiarity. Fifty-seven percent of students, regardless of classification (P=0.59), reported a disagreement in willingness to pay more for specially labeled meat products. Student perceptions towards consumption of meat and meat-type products seemed to be impacted by classification, implying as students advance through a degree program their consumer behavior is shifting. Future investigation should be conducted to evaluate additional external factors such as student knowledge as it relates to meat consumption preferences.
